openers.holocene-epoch: About 11,700 years ago, the cold of the Younger Dryas broke, and with it the Last Glacial Period and the Pleistocene ended. The abrupt warming set the remaining ice sheets of North America and Europe melting fast, and the sea jumped about 60 m in the early Holocene. Mossy forests, tundra, lakes and wetlands took over the vast mammoth steppe, and many of its giant animals died out. In the Fertile Crescent, people began growing crops and herding animals. This last stretch of the course is the world people built their history in.
openers.greenlandian-age: The Greenlandian is the opening age of the Holocene, a time of melting ice and rising water. It began when the Younger Dryas cold spell ended about 11,700 years ago, and the warming set the last northern ice sheets collapsing. Sea level jumped about 60 m between about 12,000 and 7,000 years ago, while a stronger African monsoon pushed rain far north into the Sahara. Megafauna kept dying out, and in the Fertile Crescent people began to farm and herd. At Göbekli Tepe, hunter-gatherers raised stone pillars near the time of the first permanent settlements.
openers.northgrippian-age: The Northgrippian opens with a shock: global temperatures dropped abruptly around 8,200 years ago, as Lake Agassiz drained almost completely. Off Norway, three submarine landslides moved about 3,500 km³ of debris, among the largest known. Then the warm phase reached its thermal maximum around 8,000 years BP, as the Laurentide Ice Sheet thinned and split and rising seas made Tasmania an island. William Ruddiman argues that early farmers clearing forest began raising greenhouse gases about this time. The age closes with eruptions such as Mount Mazama's, whose collapse left the caldera of Crater Lake.
openers.meghalayan-age: The youngest age of the Holocene begins with a drought: a severe one that began about 4,200 years ago and probably lasted the whole 22nd century BC. Around 4,000 years ago a major pan-tropical change dried East Africa, and the last dwarf woolly mammoths died on Wrangel Island. Great eruptions punctuate the age, from Vesuvius in the Avellino eruption to the catastrophic blast that devastated Thera. Island survivors, such as the Caribbean ground sloths, outlasted their mainland kin, while mainland thylacines vanished. The age runs on to the present day.

reviews.greenlandian-age: The Greenlandian is a single chain of cause and effect running from ice to water. The Younger Dryas ended, the northern ice sheets melted fast, and meltwater raised the sea about 60 m, drowning Doggerland and the Bering land bridge. Forests and wetlands replaced the mammoth steppe, and its giants dwindled, from the last mainland woolly mammoths to Smilodon and the American mastodon, though how far hunters were to blame is still argued. In the same warmer, wetter world, people first domesticated sheep, goats, cattle, pigs and cereals in the Fertile Crescent, and farming then rose independently from New Guinea to Mesoamerica.
reviews.northgrippian-age: The Northgrippian opened with the 8.2-kiloyear cooling, probably set off when lakes Agassiz and Ojibway flooded into the North Atlantic. Warmth returned and peaked in the Holocene Climatic Optimum, while the Laurentide Ice Sheet finally collapsed and the last land bridges to Tasmania and New Guinea drowned. As sea-level rise slowed, deltas such as the Mississippi's began to build, and farming spread into Europe. Then the long warming trend ended: neoglacial cooling began and the green Sahara dried into desert. Volcanoes such as Mazama, Kikai and Cerro Blanco, and impacts from Morasko to Henbury, marked the age's surface.
reviews.meghalayan-age: The Meghalayan began with the 4.2-kiloyear drought and has ended, so far, in a world reshaped by people. For most of it, nature set the pace: monsoons weakened, the central Sahara became a lasting desert, and eruptions from Thera to Samalas and Tambora brought volcanic winters that helped shape the Little Ice Age. People steadily added to the pressure, hunting moa, dodos and Steller's sea cow to extinction. From the Industrial Revolution on, greenhouse gases climbed, carbon dioxide passed 400 ppm at Mauna Loa, and warming, rising seas, acidifying oceans and bleaching reefs became the age's defining signals. Through it all, great earthquakes and eruptions kept reminding people of the planet's own power.

gree-004.title: Farming begins in the Fertile Crescent
gree-004.text: Barley was among the first crops: it was domesticated in the Near East around 11,000 years ago. The warming from 11.7 ka coincides with the earliest farming in the Fertile Crescent, the arc of land where crop growing and herding opened the Neolithic, the farming phase of the Stone Age. Its first farmers tamed sheep, goats, cattle and later pigs, along with cereals such as wheat and barley, and legumes. Domesticated emmer wheat appears in Iran by 9,800 BP. Between 8500 and 7000 BC people across the region took up the systematic husbandry of plants and animals. The new way of life also travelled by sea: Neolithic settlers had reached Cyprus by 8800–8600 BC. A milder climate after {{ref:gree-005}} made the change possible, and from here it spread, as {{ref:gree-029}} shows.

gree-005.title: The Younger Dryas ends and the Holocene begins
gree-005.text: Greenland's average yearly temperature rose by about 8 °C within 40 years. The jump came in three steps of five years each, and it ended the Younger Dryas, a cold spell that began about 12,800 years ago and ended about 11,700 years ago. Its close also closed the Last Glacial Period and the Pleistocene, and opened the Holocene, the epoch people still live in. Geologists mark that boundary with a GSSP, a reference point fixed in rock or ice. Here it is a sample in the NGRIP2 ice core from central Greenland, matched to the end of the Younger Dryas and ratified in 2008. After the sudden jump, global warming continued at a somewhat gentler pace through the Greenlandian. Earth has stayed in this interglacial ever since. In the American Southwest, the cool, wet pluvial climate gave way to semi-arid conditions.

gree-006.title: Forest and wetland swallow the mammoth steppe
gree-006.text: Forests replaced much of the open habitat of the large grazers as the climate turned warmer and wetter. At the start of the Holocene, mossy forests, tundra, lakes and wetlands displaced the vast mammoth steppe, the cold grassland that had fed mammoths and their neighbors. Higher temperatures and rainfall shrank that habitat, fragmenting animal populations and then driving them extinct. By about 10,000 years ago, patches of closed larch and pine forest had developed in northern Siberia. Only then did forbs, the flowering herbs that grazers ate, decline, as woody plants and grasses came to dominate.

gree-008.title: Ice Age wolf lineages collapse
gree-008.text: The wolves that howl today are not the wolves of the Ice Age. At the start of the Holocene, ancient wolves in Alaska, Siberia and Europe lost most of their genetic diversity, and they overlap little with modern wolves. In North America a population bottleneck almost erased ancient wolf diversity. One line held on far to the east: the Japanese wolf turned out to be the last of the Siberian Pleistocene wolves.

gree-001.title: The Baltic Ice Lake gives way to the Yoldia Sea
gree-001.text: The Baltic Ice Lake ended close to the start of the Holocene. Its level fell to sea level, letting salt water flow into the basin and opening the Yoldia Sea stage, about 11,700–10,700 years BP. Pine and birch pollen rose sharply around the basin from 11,500 BP, a sign of trees moving in. People followed: they lived on its Estonian shores by 11,200–10,200 BP. Next came {{ref:gree-023}}.

gree-007.title: The megafauna keep dying into the Holocene
gree-007.text: From the Late Pleistocene into the early Holocene, most animals over 45 kg vanished, including 80% of those over a tonne. Faunal density and diversity collapsed. Many megafauna species died out during the Greenlandian itself, keeping up the extinction rate of the end of the Late Pleistocene. In the Colombian Andes, spores of dung fungi, which thrive on the droppings of big grazers, record a second wave of extinction around 10,990 BP. Climate change is one main explanation, and human activity is the other. The balance between them is a long-running controversy, though most scholars accept at least some human role. Human activity is also blamed for the ongoing Holocene extinction, which began roughly 10,000 years ago.

gree-003.title: The early Holocene sea rises 60 meters
gree-003.text: Between about 12,000 and 7,000 years ago, sea level jumped about 60 m. The water came from the continental ice sheets as they melted away, as {{ref:gree-009}} describes, and the rise ran fastest while they melted. Background rates of about 6–10 mm a year were broken by brief bursts of 30–60 mm a year. Then the pace slackened, from over 10 mm a year to under 1 mm a year by 4,200 years ago. The rising water drowned vast lowlands and turned parts of continents into islands. It cut off the British Isles, Indonesia, New Guinea and Tasmania from the lands they had joined, a story told in {{ref:gree-028}} and {{ref:nort-011}}. Along Brazil's Bahia coast, mangroves followed the shoreline and spread inland as the sea rose. The modern map of coasts and straits is largely the work of these few thousand years.

gree-009.title: Northern ice sheets melt fast
gree-009.text: Most of the ice-sheet melting and sea-level rise of the last deglaciation came after about 11,000 years ago. The trigger was the abrupt warming that opened the Holocene, around 9700 BC, which set off rapid melting of the remaining ice sheets in North America and Europe. The Laurentide ice sheet's surface mass balance, the yearly gain of snow minus the loss to melting, turned negative only in the early Holocene, once radiative forcing and summer temperatures rose. In northern British Columbia, the Cordilleran ice sheet had essentially melted away by about 11,000 years ago. Later, from 8,500 BP, ice pouring from the collapsing Laurentide ice sheet made North Atlantic climate erratic.

gree-010.title: Meltwater pulse 1B: a burst that may not have been
gree-010.text: Barbados coral cores were once read as a 28 m rise in sea level in about 500 years around 11,300 years ago. That reading made Meltwater pulse 1B, a proposed burst of rapid post-glacial sea-level rise between 11,500 and 11,200 years ago, look dramatic. One study put it at 13 m in 300 years, about 40 mm a year; others cut it to 7.5 m or less than 6 m. A peak in Antarctic iceberg discharge about 11,300 years ago suggests Antarctica contributed significantly. Yet some researchers found at best a modest speed-up. Its size, and even its existence, are still debated.

gree-011.title: Hunter-gatherers raise the pillars of Göbekli Tepe
gree-011.text: Göbekli Tepe, in Upper Mesopotamia in today's Turkey, was built around 9500 BCE and used until about 8000 BCE. Its circular enclosures hold large stone pillars, among the oldest known megaliths, many carved with reliefs of wild animals. The early circles date to c. 9000 BCE. Its builders were not farmers but hunter-gatherers, who hunted gazelle and ground much cereal. Sources differ on whether any of that cereal was domesticated.

gree-015.title: The Sahara turns green
gree-015.text: From 11,000 years ago, a giant Lake Mega-Chad covered more than 350,000 km² of the Chad Basin. The cause lay in Earth's orbit. Between 11,000 and 10,000 BP, perihelion, the point where Earth passes closest to the Sun, fell at the June solstice. That raised summer sunlight by about 8% and pushed a stronger African monsoon farther north. Grasses, trees and lakes covered much of the Sahara, in a humid period that had begun about 14,600 years ago. Lake Kivu began overflowing into Lake Tanganyika by about 10,500 BP, and lakes formed in Arabia's Rub' al Khali 9,000–7,000 years ago. People moved into the greening desert: Takarkori was first occupied 10,000–9,000 years ago, and the Kiffian culture flourished 10,000–8,000 years ago.

gree-016.title: Lake Algonquin floods the upper Great Lakes
gree-016.text: Glacial Lake Algonquin first flooded about 11,000 years before present, filling the basin of the upper Great Lakes with meltwater. By then the Laurentide ice front had pulled back to the northern edges of Lakes Superior and Huron. The lake was a passing stage in the long retreat of that ice, described in {{ref:gree-009}}.

gree-017.title: South America's last notoungulates die out
gree-017.text: An order of hoofed mammals found only in South America lasted some 61 million years and then was gone. Notoungulata lived from about 61 million to 11,000 years ago. The order included Toxodon, a rhinoceros-sized grazer, which belongs among the late victims of the extinctions described in {{ref:gree-007}}.

gree-018.title: North America loses its sloths, horses and short-faced bears
gree-018.text: In Arizona's Rampart Cave, dung of the Shasta ground sloth built up from 13,000 BP and then stopped suddenly at 11,000 BP. Around that time the last giant ground sloths died out in North America, short-faced bears vanished, and all native horses disappeared. Horses had evolved largely in North America; they died out there and were reintroduced only in the 15th century. Of the continent's odd-toed hoofed mammals, only Baird's tapir, reaching into southern Mexico, survived. Ground sloths did not vanish everywhere. On Caribbean islands they lingered until about 4,000 years ago, as {{ref:megh-014}} tells.

gree-019.title: Wakamiko Caldera erupts in southern Japan
gree-019.text: Some time between 9050 and 7050 BCE, Wakamiko Caldera, nested inside Kyushu's Aira Caldera, produced an eruption of about 12 km³. It rates VEI 6 on the Volcanic Explosivity Index, the scale that ranks eruptions by the volume they throw out. The date range is wide, but the blast was among the large ones of the early Holocene.

gree-021.title: Glyptodon and its armored kin die out
gree-021.text: Glyptodon, a giant plant-eating relative of the armadillo, had lived in South America since about 3.2 million years ago, and died out around 11,000 years ago. A wetter post-glacial climate replaced C3 grasses with C4 grasses and southern beech, killing off grazing specialists such as glyptodonts and toxodonts. Human hunting may also have contributed. Its relatives Doedicurus and Panochthus held on, on the Argentine Pampas into the early Holocene, living alongside people for at least 4,000 years.

gree-020.title: The first livestock: goats, sheep, pigs and cattle
gree-020.text: By 10,000 years ago, hunters were culling young males and sparing females to breed. That simple choice marks the slide from hunting to herding. Zooarchaeology, the study of animal remains from human sites, shows that goats, pigs, sheep and taurine cattle were the first livestock, domesticated in the Fertile Crescent 11,000–10,000 years ago. The earliest dates in northern Mesopotamia are c. 9000 BCE for goats and sheep, c. 8500 BCE for pigs and c. 8000 BCE for cattle. The milder climate after the Younger Dryas made it possible. Domestication began a rapid shift in the evolution, ecology and demography of people and of many animal and plant species. It brought a cost too: in Eurasia, domestic animals overtook other primates as the main source of new human infections.

gree-023.title: The Ancylus Lake fills the Baltic basin
gree-023.text: After {{ref:gree-001}}, the land itself rose. Post-glacial uplift cut off the Baltic basin and turned it into the freshwater Ancylus Lake, from about 10,700 to 9,800 years BP. The growing lake forced people on the former Yoldia shore near Pärnu to retreat inland. It drained to the sea through the Dana River between 10,200 and 9,800 BP, and salt water began entering at 9,800 BP.

gree-031.title: The last mainland woolly mammoths
gree-031.text: Trackways at St. Mary Reservoir in Canada show a mammoth herd of adults, subadults and young still roaming there 11,300–11,000 years ago. Within a few thousand years the mainland herds were gone. In Eurasia, cold-adapted giants such as the woolly mammoth and woolly rhinoceros were generally the last of the megafauna to go, around 10,000 BP. The youngest European remains come from the Southern Urals, 9650 BCE, and Cherepovets in Russia, 9290–9180 BCE. The youngest mainland fossils of all, from Siberia's Kyttyk Peninsula, are 9,650 years old. A small population lived on much longer on Wrangel Island, as {{ref:megh-005}} tells.

gree-033.title: The modern coyote appears
gree-033.text: Not every Ice Age lineage ended in extinction. The modern coyote appeared around 10,000 years ago, most likely descended from the Pleistocene coyote. It came through the great die-off described in {{ref:gree-007}} as a smaller, newer form of an old line.

gree-032.title: The last woolly rhinoceroses
gree-032.text: The youngest woolly rhinoceros bones, from the Southern Urals, date to 9450 BCE. Its DNA lingered later in the ground: it was last detected in permafrost near Russia's Kolyma River, dated to 8050–7650 BCE. Its range had shrunk toward Siberia from 17,000 years ago. Its loss was part of the end-Pleistocene event that wiped out most large land animals.

gree-028.title: Doggerland drowns beneath the North Sea
gree-028.text: Britain was once not an island. In the early Holocene, a lowland called Doggerland linked eastern Britain to northern France, the Low Countries, north-west Germany and Jutland. Most evidence of people living there dates to the Mesolithic, the hunter-gatherer age before farming. By 9000 BCE a large tidal bay had formed between eastern England and Dogger Bank, and rapid sea-level rise followed. Between 10,000 and 7,000 years ago the rising sea broke Doggerland into low islands and then submerged it completely. Dogger Bank became an island, and Britain was finally cut off from the European mainland around 6500 BCE.

gree-029.title: Farming rises far beyond the Fertile Crescent
gree-029.text: Drainage ditches at Kuk Swamp in highland New Guinea show taro and other crops cultivated by about 11,000 BP, perhaps by 8000 BCE. The Near East was not the only cradle of farming. Between 10,000 and 7,000 BP, plants and animals were rapidly domesticated in tropical and subtropical Asia, Africa and Central America. Maize was domesticated in Mesoamerica from about 7000 BCE, and rice in the Far East. Mehrgarh in Balochistan, South Asia's earliest Neolithic site with wheat, barley and herding, is dated variously from 8500 to 6500 BCE. Cereal farming and herding reached the eastern Sahara by about 7000 BC.

gree-035.title: The Bering land bridge floods
gree-035.text: Around 8000 BCE, rising seas flooded the Beringian land bridge and closed the main migration route from Siberia. The drowning formed the Bering Strait and separated Asia from the Americas. The date is not settled. Estimates from Bering Strait depths and the global sea-level curve alone put the final drowning earlier, around 11,000 years BP. Either way, the flood was part of the rise described in {{ref:gree-003}}.

gree-038.title: The Scandinavian ice sheet melts away
gree-038.text: The Scandinavian ice sheet withdrew into the mountains as it shrank, leaving Russia by 10.6 ka and Finland by 10.1 ka. Its centre over southern Norway vanished about a thousand years after that. By 9.7 ka, the last remnant of the Fennoscandian ice sheet lay in the eastern Sarek Mountains. Freed of its weight, the land began to rise, as {{ref:gree-040}} describes.

gree-039.title: The Holocene Climatic Optimum begins
gree-039.text: Northern Hemisphere heating peaked about 9,000 years ago, when Earth's axial tilt was 24° and perihelion fell in northern summer. That timing opened the Holocene Climatic Optimum, a warm period lasting roughly from 9,500 to 5,500 years BP. The warmth did not arrive everywhere at once. In New Zealand and Antarctica the warmest stretch, often called the Early Holocene Climatic Optimum, came earlier, roughly 10,500 to 8,000 years ago. The Amery Ice Shelf in Antarctica retreated about 80 km landward during that southern warm spell. North-western North America peaked 11,000–9,000 years ago, while the Laurentide ice sheet still chilled eastern Canada. The peak itself comes in {{ref:nort-008}}.

gree-041.title: Sapropel S1 darkens the eastern Mediterranean floor
gree-041.text: Between 9,500 and 5,500 years ago, the eastern Mediterranean laid down its latest sapropel, a dark, organic-rich mud that forms when bottom waters lose oxygen. This S1 layer is tied to the African humid period. Greater Nile and other river discharge freshened the sea, stratifying it and making it eutrophic. Sapropels recur about every 21,000 years, following Earth's orbital cycles. When Nile discharge fell, deposition off its delta stopped.

gree-040.title: Scandinavia and Canada spring back
gree-040.text: Freed of ice, Scandinavia rose 9–13 mm a year between 9,500 and 5,000 years ago. Geologists call this post-glacial rebound, the slow rise of crust once a heavy ice sheet is gone. The movements triggered large earthquakes in Scandinavia about 9,000 years ago, forming postglacial faults. In Canada, the rising land drained the Champlain Sea by about 10,000 years ago. Hudson Bay, the Great Lakes and Fennoscandia are still rebounding.

gree-042.title: The last sabre-toothed Smilodon
gree-042.text: The North American Smilodon fatalis ranged from Alberta to north-western South America, and its youngest remains date to 7615–7305 BCE. Its southern cousin held out a little longer. The youngest remains of Smilodon populator, at Itapipoca in Brazil, date to 7129–6239 BCE. With them, the last Smilodon species died out.

gree-043.title: The last American mastodons
gree-043.text: Mastodons, mammoths and horses roamed North America as recently as 10,000 years ago. In Minnesota the giant animals were gone by about 9,000 years ago. The youngest remains of the American mastodon date to 7110–6810 BCE, among the last of the continent's Ice Age giants described in {{ref:gree-007}}.

gree-044.title: Today's Great Barrier Reef starts to grow
gree-044.text: The living Great Barrier Reef is younger than it looks. It is believed to have begun growing on an older platform about 9,000 years ago, as the seas of {{ref:gree-003}} rose over the land.

gree-045.title: Pluvial Lake Lahontan dries up
gree-045.text: By about 9,000 years ago, Lake Lahontan in the Great Basin had largely disappeared in its extended form. It was a pluvial lake, one fed by the wetter climate of the glacial age. Further south, tufa, a limestone crust laid down in lake water, at Lake Cahuilla records a wet period that ended 9,000 years before present.

gree-046.title: Did the Mediterranean pour into the Black Sea?
gree-046.text: A catastrophic inflow of Mediterranean seawater is proposed to have flooded the Black Sea, which was then a freshwater lake. The idea is controversial. The flood was first dated to about 7,600 years ago, then redated in 2003 to 8,800 years ago, c. 6800 BCE. Other authors argue instead for a gradual inundation of the basin. Opponents point to water flowing out of the basin as late as 15,000 years ago, and to sill sediments building up from before 10,000 years ago. The question remains open.

gree-049.title: Kurile Lake caldera blasts Kamchatka
gree-049.text: Ash from one eruption in Kamchatka fell up to 1,700 km away. In 6460–6414 BCE a very large eruption formed the present Kurile Lake caldera and its ignimbrite, a rock welded from hot volcanic ash flows. Rated VEI 7, it produced about 155 km³ of material. Two sulfate spikes in Greenland's GISP2 ice core, around 6470 and 6476 BC, may record it. It ranks with Fisher, Kikai and Mazama among the largest eruptions around the Pacific Ring of Fire, during an especially active spell in 6600–6400 BCE.

gree-005.text: A reference point fixed in a particular rock or ice layer that marks where one division of geological time begins.

gree-009.text: The yearly gain of snow on an ice sheet minus what it loses to melting.

gree-015.text: The point in Earth's orbit where it passes closest to the Sun.

gree-041.text: A dark, organic-rich mud laid down on the sea floor when bottom waters lose oxygen.

gree-040.text: The slow rise of the Earth's crust after the weight of an ice sheet is removed.

gree-049.text: Rock formed from the deposits of hot, fast-moving flows of volcanic ash and pumice.
